158.subtitle: The pith of metre, of treatise, of mantra — and the letters themselves

commentary.meaning: The verse opens with three names built on the same second element, sāra, the pith or heartwood of a thing: she is the essence of the Vedic metres, of the treatises, and of the mantras. Those three are not a random list. They are the three forms in which authoritative speech exists in this culture — the chanted hymn, the reasoned exposition, and the efficacious formula — and the claim is that whatever any of them is actually carrying, underneath its syllables and its arguments, is her. The fourth name breaks the pattern completely and describes her waist. The second line returns to praise on a large scale, her fame and her unbounded splendour, and then closes with a name that answers the three at the beginning: she takes the form of the letters. Having said that she is the pith of the metres, the treatises and the mantras, the verse ends by identifying her with the sounds those things are made of. The essence and the material turn out to be the same.
commentary.history:
Sāra is one of those Sanskrit words whose literal sense keeps its metaphor honest. It is the heartwood of a tree, the hard core left when the soft outer wood is stripped; from there it becomes the pith, the best part, the strength of anything. A tradition that calls something the sāra of a body of literature is not paying it a vague compliment but making a claim about what remains when everything removable is removed.

Chandas, the first of the three, is the Vedic word for metre and by extension for a metrical hymn, and the study of it is one of the six auxiliary disciplines a Vedic student took up alongside phonetics, grammar, etymology, ritual and astronomy. The principal metres — gāyatrī of twenty-four syllables, then uṣṇih, anuṣṭubh, bṛhatī, paṅkti, triṣṭubh and jagatī, each adding four — are not treated in the ritual literature as containers for content but as powers in their own right, associated with particular gods, particular worlds and particular effects. The ritual texts derive the word from a root meaning to cover, and explain that the gods covered themselves with the metres out of fear of death. Whatever one makes of the etymology, it records how the metres were regarded: as protective structures rather than as prosody. Calling her their sāra places her inside the oldest layer of Indian sacred speech, well behind anything specifically tantric.

Śāstra comes from √śās, to instruct or to rule — the same root as śāsana, an edict — and covers the whole range of systematic teaching, from grammar and law to medicine and erotics. To be the essence of śāstra is a different sort of claim from being the essence of the Vedas: the śāstras are human compositions, argued rather than revealed, and the name asserts that the argument arrives where the revelation does. Mantra, the third, has been characterized already in this hymn; it is worth noting only that the three names together move steadily toward compression. A hymn is long, a treatise is longer, a mantra may be a single syllable, and the verse is heading somewhere by narrowing.

Then, without transition, talodarī: she whose belly is flat as a level surface. Tala is the flat of the palm, a plane, a surface, and the compound makes a conventional claim about beauty in the conventional language of Sanskrit court poetry, where a slender waist is as standard an attribute as a lotus face. Readers new to this literature often find the shift jarring — three names about the essence of scripture, and then a compliment on her figure. It is worth resisting the impulse to allegorize it away. This hymn opened with a head-to-foot description of her body running to some forty verses, and physical epithets surface throughout precisely because the tradition does not treat her body as a metaphor for something more respectable. The commentators do offer symbolic readings of the slender waist, and those readings are worth knowing, but the plain sense is the primary one.

Udāra and uddāma, opening the second line, are both worth taking apart. Udāra means lofty, noble, generous — the word one applies to a great-hearted man as well as to an exalted reputation, so that udārakīrti says her fame is itself noble, not merely large. Uddāma is more physical: dāman is a cord or tether, the rope used to tie a calf, and ud-dāma is what has had the tether taken off. The same noun sits inside the name Dāmodara, given to Kṛṣṇa because his foster mother tied a rope around his middle. To say that her vaibhava is uddāma is to say that her magnificence has been unleashed and is running without restraint, which is a considerably more concrete image than "unbounded glory" suggests.

Varṇarūpiṇī closes the verse and closes the thought. Varṇa means a letter or speech sound; it also means colour, and it is the word for the four classes of society. The primary sense here is phonetic, and it belongs to a doctrine this hymn has already touched two verses earlier when it called her the fifty seats: the phonemes of Sanskrit, treated as a set, are themselves a goddess, Mātṛkā, and everything articulate descends from them. The suffix is the same one used in that earlier name, -rūpiṇī, she who bears the form of. What the two names together assert is that speech is not a means of referring to her. It is a portion of her, and the metres, treatises and mantras named at the head of the verse are arrangements of her own substance.
commentary.practice:
The three sāra names are the easiest sequence to garble in this verse because they differ only in their first element and share four identical final syllables. The one that needs attention is the first. Chandaḥsārā has an aspirated palatal ch at the head — a single sound, not c followed by h, and noticeably breathier than the c of caṇḍa — and then a visarga in the middle of the compound. In most recitation styles the visarga before s is realized as a light sibilant echo, so that chandaḥsārā runs together almost as chandas-sārā, with the s slightly prolonged. Do not insert a pause there; the visarga is the seam of a compound, not a break between words.

Śāstrasārā gives the cluster str, three consonants with the tongue moving from the palatal ś through a dental s to a dental t before the r taps. Say śās, then trā, and then join them without letting a vowel creep between the s and the t. Mantrasārā repeats the ntr cluster that appears throughout this hymn, dental n and dental t released into r, and the two names side by side are a good drill for the difference between the two sibilants: ś is made with the tongue toward the hard palate, s at the teeth.

Talodarī is a relief after those, four open syllables and no cluster, and it is where the breath naturally goes. Note that its o is long, as every Sanskrit o is, and that the d is dental.

The second line begins with a long compound produced by sandhi: udārakīrtiruddāmavaibhavā is udārakīrtiḥ followed by uddāmavaibhavā, with the visarga of the first turning into r before the vowel that begins the second. Knowing this is what keeps the line from being an unbroken block of sound. The doubled d of uddāma must be held — a geminate consonant in Sanskrit takes real time, and clipping it makes the word into udāma, which is not a word here. Say ud, hold, then dāma.

Varṇarūpiṇī has two retroflex nasals, one in varṇa and one in rūpiṇī, and both are there because of a preceding r. Curl the tongue back and keep it back through the vowel that follows.

For archanā the datives are chandaḥsārāyai, śāstrasārāyai, mantrasārāyai, talodaryai, udārakīrtaye, uddāmavaibhavāyai and varṇarūpiṇyai. Udārakīrtiḥ is the irregular one: kīrti is an i-stem, so the dative is kīrtaye and not the expected -āyai, exactly like prakaṭākṛtaye three verses earlier. Two i-stems in four verses is not many, and both of them are easy to regularize by mistake.

The verse also has something to say about the act being performed while it is recited. A person chanting this line is using metre, is repeating what a treatise has fixed, is producing sounds treated as mantra, and is doing all of it with letters. The verse names the essence of each of those four things and identifies it with the person being addressed, which means that by the time the reciter reaches varṇarūpiṇī there is nothing left in the situation — not the medium, not the method, not the material — that has been left outside her.

crossReferences.deva: तस्माद्यज्ञात्सर्वहुत ऋचः सामानि जज्ञिरे । छन्दांसि जज्ञिरे तस्माद्यजुस्तस्मादजायत ॥
crossReferences.iast: tasmād yajñāt sarvahuta ṛcaḥ sāmāni jajñire | chandāṃsi jajñire tasmād yajus tasmād ajāyata ||
crossReferences.translation: From that sacrifice, in which everything was offered, the verses and the chants were born. The metres were born from it; from it the sacrificial formula was born.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest statement of where the metres come from, and it puts them among the first things produced when the cosmic person is offered up. Chandaḥsārā presupposes exactly this status: the metres are not literary conventions but constituents of the world, which is why identifying their pith with the goddess is a cosmological claim and not a compliment to poetry.

crossReferences.deva: अहं रुद्रेभिर्वसुभिश्चराम्यहमादित्यैरुत विश्वदेवैः । अहं मित्रावरुणोभा बिभर्म्यहमिन्द्राग्नी अहमश्विनोभा ॥
crossReferences.iast: ahaṃ rudrebhir vasubhiś carāmy aham ādityair uta viśvadevaiḥ | ahaṃ mitrāvaruṇobhā bibharmy aham indrāgnī aham aśvinobhā ||
crossReferences.translation: I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, I with the Ādityas and All-Gods. I carry both Mitra and Varuṇa, I both Indra and Agni, I both Aśvins.
crossReferences.relevance: Speech herself is the speaker of this hymn, and she claims to carry the gods rather than to describe them. The Śākta tradition has read the passage as its own charter, and varṇarūpiṇī is the sahasranāma's condensed form of it: if the goddess is embodied as the letters, then every hymn addressed to any god is being conducted through her.

crossReferences.deva: बृहत्साम तथा साम्नां गायत्री छन्दसामहम् । मासानां मार्गशीर्षोऽहमृतूनां कुसुमाकरः ॥
crossReferences.iast: bṛhatsāma tathā sāmnāṃ gāyatrī chandasām aham | māsānāṃ mārgaśīrṣo 'ham ṛtūnāṃ kusumākaraḥ ||
crossReferences.translation: Of the chants I am the Bṛhat Sāman, of the metres the Gāyatrī; of the months I am Mārgaśīrṣa, of the seasons the flowering spring.
crossReferences.relevance: The Gītā's long list of superlatives works by naming the best item within each class, and its formula for the metres is the closest structural parallel to chandaḥsārā. The difference is instructive: the Gītā picks out one metre as its representative, while the sahasranāma claims the pith common to all of them, which is a stronger and less pictorial move.

references.title: The Rigveda: The Earliest Religious Poetry of India
references.author: Stephanie W. Jamison and Joel P. Brereton (Oxford University Press, 2014)
references.note: The complete translation that supersedes everything before it, with introductions to each hymn that explain what is going on rather than gesturing at it. Read the Puruṣa hymn and the hymn of Speech in it before deciding what chandaḥsārā and varṇarūpiṇī are claiming.

references.title: A Vedic Grammar for Students
references.author: Arthur Anthony Macdonell (Oxford, 1916)
references.note: Small, cheap, still in print, and its appendix on Vedic metre is the most efficient introduction to the subject in English. Twenty pages will teach you to hear the difference between an anuṣṭubh and a triṣṭubh, after which the first name in this verse stops being abstract.

references.title: Vāc: The Concept of the Word in Selected Hindu Tantras
references.author: André Padoux, tr. Jacques Gontier (SUNY Press, 1990)
references.note: The standard study of speech as cosmic substance, and the book that makes sense of a deity being identified with the alphabet. Its treatment of the mātṛkā, the phonemes taken as a goddess, is directly behind varṇarūpiṇī.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma with Bhāskararāya's Commentary
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library and Research Centre)
references.note: Worth consulting here for talodarī, where the commentarial tradition offers symbolic readings of the slender waist alongside the literal one. Seeing how a learned reader handles a physical epithet in the middle of a doctrinal sequence is instructive whether or not you follow him.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Look up dāman and then uddāma. Seeing that the second is built on the ordinary word for the rope used to tie up a calf turns a stock phrase about unbounded glory into a specific image, and that kind of recovery is most of what a dictionary is for in this hymn.
